contentHtml:
Cancer therapy is rapidly changing and a new therapeutic modality is coming to the forefront of cancer treatment, moving along the lines of various immunotherapy, targeted therapies, precision medicine, as well as some new drug combinations. Accessing the therapies is not always possible. New therapies are initially assessed through clinical trials, making it possible to assess their safety, effectiveness and potential advantage over other therapies… Participation in a clinical trial gives patients access to new therapies and possibilities but this depends on the eligibility criteria for the trial, discovering the location of the trial, its cost and other issues.

The concepts of clinical trials in cancer treatment

Clinical trials are studies aimed at testing new cancer treatments, diagnostic approaches or methods of treatment. The trials help to determine whether the treatment is more effective and less harmful than other methods.

There are various phases involved in the cancer clinical trials. Phase I trials involve mainly checking the safety of a particular treatment and determining the right dosage levels. In Phase II trials, the efficacy of the treatment is assessed in different types of cancer while Phase III trials are conducted in which the newer medicine is compared with the conventional medicines. The last phase of clinical trials, i.e., Phase IV phase, involves analyzing the long-term effects of the medicine once it is approved.

Not every clinical trial makes use of a brand new medicine. Some trials involve the testing of combinations of different existing medicines or testing application of different procedures.

Patient eligibility: The first barrier to access

Patient eligibility is the main factor influencing participation in cancer clinical trials. Each trial will have inclusion criteria and exclusion criteria set up to ensure patient safety and create meaningful results.

All these criteria could include cancer type and stage, previously received therapies, age, general health condition, organ functioning, genetic mutations and other medical conditions of the patient. For instance, if the trial is looking for a targeted therapy, only patients whose tumors have a specific mutation will be invited. In addition, there are trials where only patients who have failed the standard treatment will be accepted while some trials only accept patients who have just recently been diagnosed with cancer.

Even though these criteria are important for medicine, they reduce the number of patients eligible for the trial. A patient may want to join the trial but will not be able to do it due to his stage of disease, therapy already received, or other health problems.

Awareness and timely referral make a difference

Another great obstacle is lack of awareness. Many patients as well as caregivers have little knowledge of clinical trials or think that they can be used only after all other therapies have failed.

In fact, clinical trials can be offered at various stages of a cancer treatment depending on the subject being researched. Some studies involve patients who were just diagnosed with cancer whereas others deal with cases of advanced or treatment-resistant cancers.

The timing of patients’ referral is of great significance. There are studies that look for patients at particular stages of cancer treatment. If patients learn about the study too late, they will not meet its requirements.

Oncologists play a significant part in finding appropriate studies and explaining them to patients. Additionally, hospitals with clinical research teams can help patients in understanding available trials and getting assessed for eligibility.

Geographic location and hospital infrastructure

The access to the clinical trials is dependent on where the patients are treated. Most cancer based trials take place at some of the major hospitals, leading academic medical centres and specialised research institutions having all infrastructure, regulatory approvals which are needed to conduct the trials.

This can lead to problems for patients in the small towns and rural areas as they have to travel to major centres for screening, treatment, follow-ups and monitoring.

The travelling cost and time away from home makes it difficult to participate in trial even where it is available.

The research capabilities should be expanded beyond large metropolitan hospitals to address this problem. Better co-operations between legal hospitals and cancer centres can help improve patient access.

Financial considerations and associated costs

Despite the fact that clinical trial medications and specific research-related duties are usually provided by the sponsor of the study in accordance with the study procedure, being involved in the study does not always mean that all expenses associated with the treatment apply to the medications received. In different trials, patients have to pay for the routine health care services, customary procedures, travelling and lodging depending on the terms of the study. For those people travelling far, such indirect costs can constitute a substantial burden.

Also, reimbursement and compensation rules can affect the choice of whether to take part in the trial. Patients should be aware of the expenses covered by the trial, those related to routine cancer treatment and whether there are other expenses that may emerge.

It is advisable to let the participants and their families know about the financial liabilities before the study starts.

Genetic testing and precision medicine

The increasing significance of precision oncology is paved way for various opportunities in taking part in clinical trials. Many of the recent cancer therapies have been developed to target particular genetic alterations or molecular features of the tumor, unlike traditional approaches which relied on the organ of origin.

However, the identification of the candidates necessitates access to molecular profiling and next-generation sequencing tests. These tests facilitate the understanding of the biological characteristics of a tumor, as well as the qualification of a particular patient for a targeted treatment clinical trial.

Nevertheless, the main issue that has to be dealt with is the availability of advanced testing. The reasons for challenge include disparities in cost, existence of specialized laboratories as well as knowledge of biomarker-driven clinical research.

Implementing molecular diagnostics into the process of cancer treatment provides an opportunity to identify patients that fit the eligibility criteria for clinical trials.

Informed consent and patient safety

Any clinical trial must always be accompanied by a firm understanding of the possible advantages as well as drawbacks featured in it. Patients should participate voluntarily and give their consent before being enrolled.

A physician must clarify purposes of the trial, treatment under investigation, side effects and other treatment alternatives, as well as expected follow-ups and rights of the patients to drop out of the trial at any time and still get all standard treatment options.

Clinical trials operate according to regulatory and ethical principles in order to ensure complete safety of the participants. Independent committees assess the protocol of the trial while doctors are in charge of monitoring participants over possible complications.

It should be remembered that experimental treatment does not mean it is better than available therapy. As a result, participation in the clinical trial does not ensure better results.

Strengthening clinical trial access in India

To achieve improvement in access to cancer clinical trials, one needs to coordinate the efforts of various stakeholders including hospitals, researchers, drug manufacturers, regulatory authorities and healthcare policymakers. Programs to increase participation should involve better awareness among patients and oncologists, as well as the improvement of research-oriented hospitals, access to molecular diagnostics and establishment of strong referral systems.

Moreover, by enhancing the infrastructure of clinical trials and creating a bigger number of investigator-sponsored studies, India is in a good position to improve its position in oncology research, because of the necessity of participation of various patient groups in the trials. Distribution of clinical trial centers and patient support systems according to the geographical position may also improve access to the trials.

In any case, clinical trials are an important part of innovation in cancer therapy. However, besides contributing to the creation of new medications, clinical trials provide us with new data and knowledge and create opportunities for patients of the future.
